title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 149
paragraphs: So the Council replied, they say, even though the oracle had forbidden them to make the alliance with the Greeks. They were eager, they say, for a thirty-year truce from hostilities, despite their fear of the oracle, so that (as they allege) their sons might grow to manhood during those years; they feared that if there was no truce and another disaster befell them fighting the Persian on top of the one they had already suffered, they might for all time to come be subject to the Lacedaemonians. To what the Council said, those of the envoys who were from Sparta replied that regarding the truce they would refer the matter to their public assembly, but regarding the leadership they were themselves empowered to answer, and they did so: they had two kings, while the Argives had one; it was not possible to remove either of the two Spartan kings from leadership, but nothing prevented the Argive king from having an equal vote with each of theirs. Then, say the Argives, they could not bear the grasping selfishness of the Spartans; they chose to be ruled by the barbarians rather than yield in any way to the Lacedaemonians, and they ordered the envoys to leave the territory of Argos before sunset, or else be treated as enemies.
